title: Building Models: The First Task for a Strong MGC Game (Plus Other First-Week Insights) ek-insights/
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart shares first-week observations from using his Tracking Attempted Moments of Genuine Connection (MGC) strategy from The Will to Learn. He argues that the first job of a strong MGC game is building working mental models of each student, which starts with attaching names to faces and is both tiring and enjoyable. He insists the tracking system stay simple, because teachers who over-complicate it see it collapse. He answers the objection that tracking takes the magic out of connection by saying it creates regular, systematic room for magic. The key stance is that the attempt matters, not whether any single moment worked, so the teacher's job is the inner work of valuing, knowing and respecting every student. He also notes that MGCs build credibility and belonging and lay the relational base for harder strategies like Woodenization and Valued Within exercises.
points: Start the year by building a working mental model of each student, beginning with names and faces and growing from there.
Keep the tracking system deliberately simple, since complexity is the main reason teachers' MGC efforts break down.
Judge the practice by the attempt rather than the outcome, trusting that frequent genuine attempts will get through to students.
Tracking does not kill the magic of connection; it guarantees regular room for it.
MGCs do several jobs at once, building credibility and belonging and creating the relational base for harder teaching moves.
quotes: This model-building work — which starts with simply attaching names to faces and grows from there — is, to me, one of the primary sources of both exhaustion and pleasure during the first couple weeks of school. It’s something I have to both work and play at.
The more complex the system, the more likely it is to break down. For me, it must be kept simple.

Sometimes folks complain that tracking attempted MGCs takes the magic out of building connections with students. But to me, tracking attempted MGCs just means I’m making regular, systematic room for lots of magic to take place.

The point is the attempt, not the outcome. I spend exactly zero seconds wondering whether or not a given MGC “worked.” The fact is, MGCs will work when conducted often enough, so long as I make sure I’m working hard to genuinely value, know, and respect each of my students.
And, make no mistake: it takes hard inner work for me to like some of my students in this way. But the work is worth it.

So long as you’re doing this, you don’t need to worry about whether or not a student “felt” how you feel about them. Just keep at it; they’re smart and receptive, and the signal will get through eventually.
